title: The early hours
hookLine: the ambrosial hours before dawn, praised in Japji's fourth pauri

cards: There's an hour most of us only meet by accident. The flight that leaves at six. The baby who won't settle.
The night you couldn't sleep, finally gave up, and made tea. The house is silent. No messages, because everyone you know is asleep.
Even the birds haven't started. It feels strange, a little lonely, and oddly clean. Sikhs have a name for that hour, and they don't treat it as an accident.
They treat it as a gift, and some Sikhs set an alarm for it.

teach.b: The name is amrit vela. Vela means time, or hour. Amrit is nectar, the drink of immortality in old Indian stories, the thing that makes life deathless.
So amrit vela is the nectar hour, often translated the ambrosial hour: the last watch of the night, before dawn. The text gives no clock time for it.
It comes from Japji, Guru Nanak's morning hymn, the same fourth pauri where you met nadar, grace, on day one hundred eighteen.
There he asks what we can offer to the One who gives everything, and answers: in the ambrosial hours, contemplate the true Name and its greatness. That's the whole instruction. No ritual, no list.

teach.h: THE NAME, IN THE EARLY HOUR.
teach.b: Just the Name, in the early hour.

Later, Guru Ram Das describes a Sikh's day, in paraphrase: one who calls himself a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and meditates on the Name, bathes, and keeps remembering through the day. Why so early?
Sikh writers give a few reasons. The mind is quieter before the world starts pulling on it. The day hasn't made any claims yet, so the first thing it hears is the Name.
And there's something honest about giving up a little sleep: it costs something.

In many Sikh homes and gurdwaras the day really does begin this way, with Nitnem and simran in the dark, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar the Guru Granth Sahib is brought out in procession before dawn.
Nobody has to become a monk to try it. Five minutes counts.

how: Many Sikhs rise in the amrit vela, the hours before dawn, to bathe, recite the morning banis and do simran before the day's work begins.

practice: Picture your alarm set five minutes earlier for tomorrow, or set it now if you like.

Then close your eyes and imagine those extra five minutes: the dark room, the quiet, the breath, and, if you pray, a word like Waheguru before anything else gets in; if you're here to learn, simply sit with the silence.
